otin R$, so $R$ is not symmetric; and $(1,3),(3,2)\in R$ but $(1,2)
otin R$, so it is not transitive.
useful_results: $\gcd(a,a)=|a|$, so a $\gcd$-type relation is reflexive only at $a=\pm1$; it can never be reflexive on all of $\mathbb{Z}$.

If a relation is defined by a formula that is symmetric in $(a,b)$ AND an extra asymmetric condition (like $2a\neq b$, $a<b$, $a=2b$), symmetry fails; look for a pair where the extra condition kills only one direction.
To disprove transitivity find a chain $a\to b\to c$ with $(a,c)$ forbidden; here the forbidden pair is $(1,2)$ and any odd $b\ne1$ works as the middle (check $b=5$: $(1,5),(5,2)\in R$).
One counterexample disproves a property; proving it needs an argument for all elements.

questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation defined on $\mathbb{N}$ as $a\,R\,b$ if $2a+3b$ is a multiple of $5$, $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$. Then $R$ is : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: $2a+3b=5b+2(a-b)$, so $a\,R\,b$ is just $a\equiv b\pmod 5$; test the three properties directly.
solution: Reflexive: for $(a,a)$, $2a+3a=5a$, which is divisible by $5$. So $(a,a)\in R$ for all $a\in\mathbb{N}$ and $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: let $(a,b)\in R$, so $2a+3b=5k_1$. Also $5a+5b=5k_2$.
Subtracting: $5a+5b-2a-3b=5(k_2-k_1)$, i.e. $3a+2b=5(k_2-k_1)$, which is $2b+3a=5k$. So $(b,a)\in R$ and $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive: let $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$, so $2a+3b=5k_1$ and $2b+3c=5k_2$.
Adding: $2a+3b+2b+3c=5(k_1+k_2)$, so $2a+3c=5(k_1+k_2)-5b=5\lambda$ with $\lambda=k_1+k_2-b$.
So $(a,c)\in R$ and $R$ is transitive.
$R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite $2a+3b=2(a-b)+5b$, so $5\mid 2a+3b\iff5\mid(a-b)$ because $\gcd(2,5)=1$: $R$ is congruence mod $5$.
solution: $2a+3b=2(a-b)+5b$, so $5\mid(2a+3b)\iff5\mid2(a-b)$.
Since $5$ is prime and does not divide $2$, $5\mid2(a-b)\iff5\mid(a-b)$.
Hence $a\,R\,b\iff a\equiv b\pmod5$.
Congruence modulo $5$ is reflexive ($a-a=0$), symmetric ($5\mid a-b\Rightarrow5\mid b-a$) and transitive ($5\mid a-b,\ 5\mid b-c\Rightarrow5\mid a-c$).
So $R$ is an equivalence relation (with $5$ classes, by remainders $0,1,2,3,4$): option (B).

useful_results: $a\,R\,b\iff pa+qb\equiv0\pmod m$ is an equivalence relation when $p+q\equiv0\pmod m$ (then it is $p(a-b)\equiv0$). Check $m=5,p=2,q=3$; for $2a+3b\bmod7$, $(1,1)$ gives $5$, so it is not reflexive.
If also $\gcd(p,m)=1$, the relation is exactly $a\equiv b\pmod m$ and has $m$ equivalence classes.
Quick reflexivity test for linear-condition relations: substitute $b=a$; the condition should hold for all $a$.
Congruence mod $m$ is the model equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{N}$; its classes are the remainder classes.

concepts: Types of relations (symmetric and transitive closure)
questions.question: The minimum number of elements that must be added to the relation $R=\{(a,b),(b,c)\}$ on the set $\{a,b,c\}$ so that it becomes symmetric and transitive is : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: Symmetry gives $(b,a),(c,b)$; transitivity then forces $(a,c),(c,a)$ and the reflexive pairs, i.e. the full $3\times3$ relation.
solution: For symmetric: $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$ forces $(b,a),(c,b)\in R$.
For transitive: $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$ forces $(a,c)\in R$.
Now symmetric again: $(a,c)\in R$ forces $(c,a)\in R$.
Transitive again: $(a,b),(b,a)\in R$ forces $(a,a)\in R$; also $(b,c),(c,b)\in R$ forces $(b,b)\in R$ and $(c,c)\in R$.
Elements to be added: $(b,a),(c,b),(a,c),(c,a),(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$.
Each of these is forced, and the resulting relation is all $9$ pairs, which is symmetric and transitive.
Number of elements to be added $=7$ (that is $9-2$): option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: A symmetric transitive relation links $a,b,c$ into one class, so it must contain every pair of $\{a,b,c\}$: $3^2=9$ pairs.
solution: In a symmetric and transitive relation, $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ give $a\sim c$, so $a,b,c$ are all related to each other.
For any related $x\sim y$ symmetry gives $y\sim x$ and transitivity gives $x\sim x$; so every $(x,y)$ with $x,y\in\{a,b,c\}$ is forced.
The relation must therefore be all $3\times3=9$ ordered pairs, and this relation is indeed symmetric and transitive.
$R$ already has $2$ pairs, so $9-2=7$ must be added: option (A).

useful_results: A symmetric and transitive relation is reflexive on every element that appears in some pair: $(x,y)\in R\Rightarrow(y,x)\in R\Rightarrow(x,x)\in R$.

The smallest symmetric transitive relation containing $R$ is $\bigcup C_i\times C_i$ over the connected components $C_i$ of the graph of $R$; its size is $\sum|C_i|^2$ (here one component of $3$ elements: $9$).
The smallest equivalence relation containing $R$ also adds $(x,x)$ for elements in no pair; it has $\sum|C_i|^2$ pairs with isolated points as components of size $1$.
The symmetric-transitive-but-not-reflexive example: the empty relation on a set, or $\{(a,a)\}$ on $\{a,b\}$.

questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ defined by $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ if and only if $ad(b-c)=bc(a-d)$. Then $R$ is : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
options: symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
transitive but neither reflexive nor symmetric
questions.answer: (A) symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $abcd$ turns the condition into $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1d-\frac1c$, i.e. the two 'differences' are negatives of each other.
solution: $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)\iff\frac{b-c}{bc}=\frac{a-d}{ad}$ (divide $ad(b-c)=bc(a-d)$ by $abcd$).
So $\frac1c-\frac1b=\frac1d-\frac1a$, which rearranges to $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1d-\frac1c$.
Reflexive: $(a,b)\,R\,(a,b)$ would need $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1b-\frac1a$, i.e. $a=b$. This is false for $a\ne b$ (e.g. $(1,2)$). Not reflexive.
Symmetric: $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ gives $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1d-\frac1c$. Multiplying by $-1$: $\frac1c-\frac1d=\frac1b-\frac1a$, which is the condition for $(c,d)\,R\,(a,b)$. Symmetric.
Transitive: $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ gives $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1d-\frac1c$, and $(c,d)\,R\,(e,f)$ gives $\frac1c-\frac1d=\frac1f-\frac1e$.
Together these give $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1e-\frac1f$, which is not the condition $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1f-\frac1e$ for $(a,b)\,R\,(e,f)$ unless both sides are $0$. Not transitive in general.
Example: $(1,2)\,R\,(2,1)$ and $(2,1)\,R\,(1,2)$, but $(1,2)\,R\,(1,2)$ fails. Hence $R$ is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the polynomial condition $ad(b-c)=bc(a-d)$ directly: swapping the two pairs gives the same equation, and small integer pairs refute the other two properties.
solution: Symmetric: $(c,d)\,R\,(a,b)$ means $cb(d-a)=da(c-b)$. Multiplying by $-1$ gives $bc(a-d)=ad(b-c)$, the original equation. So $R$ is symmetric.
Reflexive: $(a,b)\,R\,(a,b)$ means $ab(b-a)=ba(a-b)$, i.e. $2ab(b-a)=0$, false for $(1,2)$ (it gives $4\ne0$).
Test $(1,2)\,R\,(2,1)$: $ad(b-c)=1\cdot1\cdot(2-2)=0$ and $bc(a-d)=2\cdot2\cdot(1-1)=0$. True.
By symmetry $(2,1)\,R\,(1,2)$ is also true. If $R$ were transitive then $(1,2)\,R\,(1,2)$, which was shown false.
So $R$ is symmetric, not reflexive and not transitive: option (A).

useful_results: Divide a relation defined by a product identity by the product of the variables ($abcd$ here) to reveal a hidden difference or ratio form: $\frac{b-c}{bc}=\frac1c-\frac1b$.
A relation $f(x)=f(y)$ is always an equivalence relation (classes = level sets of $f$); but $f(x)=-f(y)$, i.e. $f(x)+f(y)=0$, is symmetric and in general neither reflexive nor transitive.
$f(x)=-f(y)$ is reflexive only where $f(x)=0$ and is transitive only if $f=0$ on the elements involved (here $f(a,b)=\frac1a-\frac1b$ vanishes iff $a=b$).
For pair-relations on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, test small points such as $(1,2),(2,1)$ before attempting a general proof.

questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb{R}$, given by $R=\{(a,b) : 3a-3b+\sqrt7\text{ is an irrational number}\}$. Then $R$ is : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.answer: (B) reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
questions.key_idea: $(a,b)\in R$ depends on $3(a-b)+\sqrt7$, so choose $a-b$ so that this expression is rational in one direction only.
solution: Reflexive: $3(a-a)+\sqrt7=\sqrt7$, which is irrational, so $(a,a)\in R$ for every $a$. $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: take $a=\frac{\sqrt7}{3}$, $b=0$. Then $3a-3b+\sqrt7=2\sqrt7$, irrational, so $(a,b)\in R$.
But $3(b-a)+\sqrt7=-\sqrt7+\sqrt7=0$, which is rational, so $(b,a)\notin R$. Hence $R$ is not symmetric.
Transitive: take $(a,b)=\left(\frac{\sqrt7}{3},1\right)$: $\sqrt7-3+\sqrt7=2\sqrt7-3$, irrational, so $(a,b)\in R$.
Take $(b,c)=\left(1,\frac{2\sqrt7}{3}\right)$: $3-2\sqrt7+\sqrt7=3-\sqrt7$, irrational, so $(b,c)\in R$.
For $(a,c)=\left(\frac{\sqrt7}{3},\frac{2\sqrt7}{3}\right)$: $\sqrt7-2\sqrt7+\sqrt7=0$, rational, so $(a,c)\notin R$. Hence $R$ is not transitive.
So $R$ is reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: $R$ depends only on $d=a-b$: $R$ holds iff $d\in D$ where $D=\{d:3d+\sqrt7\notin\mathbb{Q}\}$. Reflexive iff $0\in D$, symmetric iff $D=-D$, transitive iff $D+D\subseteq D$.
solution: $(a,b)\in R\iff d=a-b\in D$, where $D$ is $\mathbb{R}$ minus the set $E=\left\{\frac{q-\sqrt7}{3}:q\in\mathbb{Q}\right\}$.
Reflexive: $a-a=0\in D$ because $3\cdot0+\sqrt7=\sqrt7$ is irrational ($0\notin E$).
Symmetric needs $d\in D\Rightarrow-d\in D$. Take $d=\frac{\sqrt7}{3}$: $3d+\sqrt7=2\sqrt7$ irrational, so $d\in D$; but $-d=-\frac{\sqrt7}{3}\in E$ (take $q=0$), so $-d\notin D$. Not symmetric.
Transitive needs $x,y\in D\Rightarrow x+y\in D$. Take $x=y=-\frac{\sqrt7}{6}$: $3x+\sqrt7=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}$ is irrational, so $x,y\in D$.
But $x+y=-\frac{\sqrt7}{3}\in E$, so $x+y\notin D$. E.g. $(a,b,c)=\left(-\frac{\sqrt7}{3},-\frac{\sqrt7}{6},0\right)$ gives $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$ and $(a,c)\notin R$. Not transitive.
So $R$ is reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive: option (B).

useful_results: If $a\,R\,b$ depends only on $d=a-b$ through a set $D$: reflexive iff $0\in D$; symmetric iff $D=-D$; transitive iff $D+D\subseteq D$. Check $D=\mathbb{Z}$ (equivalence) and $D=(0,\infty)$ (transitive only).
For a rational $q$: $q+\sqrt7$ is irrational, and $r\sqrt7$ is irrational for rational $r\ne0$; use these to decide when an expression is rational.
In 'irrational/rational' relations, build counterexamples with multiples of $\sqrt7$ so that sums cancel to exactly $0$ (rational) in one direction.
Reflexivity of 'expression in $a-b$' relations is just evaluation at $0$.

concepts: Cardinality of a set defined by an equation
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x : x\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)^{x^2-4}+\left(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)^{x^2-4}=10\right\}$. Then $n(S)$ is equal to : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)=1$ makes the two terms reciprocal, so $t+\frac1t=10$ with $t=5\pm2\sqrt6$.
solution: Square the base: $\left(\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2\right)^2=5\pm2\sqrt6$. So the equation is $\left(5+2\sqrt6\right)^{\frac{x^2-4}{2}}+\left(5-2\sqrt6\right)^{\frac{x^2-4}{2}}=10$.
Now $\left(5+2\sqrt6\right)\left(5-2\sqrt6\right)=25-24=1$, so the two bases are reciprocals.
Also $\left(5+2\sqrt6\right)+\left(5-2\sqrt6\right)=10$.
With $t=\left(5+2\sqrt6\right)^{\frac{x^2-4}{2}}$ the equation is $t+\frac1t=10$, so $t=5\pm2\sqrt6$ (roots of $t^2-10t+1=0$).
$x^2=6$ or $x^2=2$, so $x=\pm\sqrt6,\ \pm\sqrt2$.
Therefore $n(S)=4$: option (D).
useful_results: $(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)=a-b$; when $a-b=1$ the two surds are reciprocal, so $p^u+p^{-u}=k$ becomes $t+\frac1t=k$ with $t=p^u$.
$t+\frac1t=k\Rightarrow t=\frac{k\pm\sqrt{k^2-4}}{2}$ (real positive roots need $k\ge2$); for $k=10$, $t=5\pm2\sqrt6$ (check $5+2\sqrt6\approx9.899$, $+\frac1t\approx0.101$, sum $10$).
$\left(\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2\right)^2=5\pm2\sqrt6$; in general $(\sqrt a\pm\sqrt b)^2=a+b\pm2\sqrt{ab}$.
The map $u\mapsto p^u+p^{-u}$ is even, so solutions of $p^u+p^{-u}=k$ come in pairs $u=\pm u_0$; remember each $x^2=c>0$ then gives two real $x$.

questions.question: Let $P(S)$ denote the power set of $S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,10\}$. Define the relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ on $P(S)$ as $A\,R_1\,B$ if $(A\cap B^C)\cup(B\cap A^C)=\phi$ and $A\,R_2\,B$ if $A\cup B^C=B\cup A^C$, $\forall A,B\in P(S)$. Then : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
options: both $R_1$ and $R_2$ are not equivalence relations
questions.key_idea: Each relation forces the 'only-in-$A$' and 'only-in-$B$' Venn regions to be empty, so each is just $A=B$.
solution: $A\,R_1\,B\iff(A\cap B^C)\cup(A^C\cap B)=\phi$. Use the Venn regions: $a=A\cap B^C$, $b=A^C\cap B$, $c=A\cap B$, $d=A^C\cap B^C$.
$R_1$ is reflexive ($A\cap A^C=\phi$) and symmetric (the condition is unchanged on swapping $A,B$).
Transitive: $A\,R_1\,B$ means regions $a$ and $b$ are both empty, so $A=B$. Likewise $B\,R_1\,C$ gives $B=C$.
Hence $A=C$, so $(A\cap C^C)\cup(A^C\cap C)=\phi$ and $A\,R_1\,C$. So $R_1$ is an equivalence relation.
$R_2$: $A\,R_2\,B\iff A\cup B^C=B\cup A^C$. It is reflexive ($A\cup A^C=A\cup A^C$) and symmetric (equality is symmetric).
Transitive: in the Venn regions $A\cup B^C=\{a,c,d\}$ and $B\cup A^C=\{b,c,d\}$. Equality forces $\{a\}=\{b\}$; the regions are disjoint, so both are empty and $A=B$.
Similarly $B\,R_2\,C$ gives $B=C$, hence $A=C$ and $A\cup C^C=C\cup A^C$, i.e. $A\,R_2\,C$. So $R_2$ is an equivalence relation.
Both $R_1$ and $R_2$ are equivalence relations: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Show that both $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the identity relation $A=B$, which is trivially an equivalence relation.
solution: $(A\cap B^C)\cup(B\cap A^C)=A\,\triangle\,B$, and $A\,\triangle\,B=\phi\iff A=B$. So $R_1$ is the relation $A=B$.
Take complements in $A\cup B^C=B\cup A^C$: $A^C\cap B=B^C\cap A$, i.e. $B-A=A-B$.
The sets $B-A$ and $A-B$ are disjoint, so being equal they are both empty: $B\subseteq A$ and $A\subseteq B$, i.e. $A=B$.
Conversely $A=B$ clearly satisfies $A\cup B^C=B\cup A^C$. So $R_2$ is also the relation $A=B$.
Equality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (classes are the $2^{10}$ singletons of $P(S)$), so both relations are equivalence relations: option (B).

useful_results: $(A\cap B^C)\cup(A^C\cap B)=A\triangle B$, and $A\triangle B=\phi\iff A=B$.
Complement trick: $A\cup B^C=B\cup A^C\iff A^C\cap B=A\cap B^C\iff A=B$ (both differences are disjoint, so both must be empty). Brute-force checked for $|S|=3$ and $4$.
Relations that reduce to equality are equivalence relations whose classes are single elements; here there are $|P(S)|=2^{10}=1024$ classes.
Related equivalence: $A\cup X=B\cup X\iff A-X=B-X$ for a fixed $X$, with $2^{|S|-|X|}$ classes (check $S=\{1,2\},X=\{1\}$: $2$ classes).

questions.question: The minimum number of elements that must be added to the relation $R=\{(a,b),(b,c),(b,d)\}$ on the set $\{a,b,c,d\}$ so that it is an equivalence relation, is ______. [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: $b$ is linked to $a$, $c$, $d$, so all four elements end up in a single class and the relation must be all $4^2=16$ pairs.
solution: To make it an equivalence relation on this set, $R$ must contain the reflexive pairs $(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(d,d)$.
By symmetry it must contain $(b,a),(c,b),(d,b)$ in addition to $(a,b),(b,c),(b,d)$.
By transitivity through $b$: $(a,b),(b,c)\Rightarrow(a,c)$; $(a,b),(b,d)\Rightarrow(a,d)$; $(c,b),(b,d)\Rightarrow(c,d)$; and their reverses $(c,a),(d,a),(d,c)$ by symmetry.
$3$ of these are already given, so $16-3=13$ elements must be added.

alternate_solutions.idea: An equivalence relation is the same as a partition into classes; $b$ is related to $a,c,d$ so there is just one class $\{a,b,c,d\}$, giving $4^2$ pairs.
solution: Any equivalence relation containing $R$ has $a\sim b$, $b\sim c$ and $b\sim d$, so $a,b,c,d$ lie in one equivalence class.
The only equivalence relation with one class on a $4$-element set is $\{a,b,c,d\}\times\{a,b,c,d\}$, with $4^2=16$ pairs, so the minimal (and only) choice has $16$ pairs.
$R$ already supplies $3$ pairs, so the number to be added is $16-3=13$.

useful_results: An equivalence relation on a set is the same as a partition of it into classes; a class with $k$ elements contributes $k^2$ ordered pairs.

The smallest equivalence relation containing $R$ is built from the connected components of the graph of $R$ (ignoring direction): size $\sum k_i^2$, so the number to add is $\sum k_i^2-|R|$ (here $16-3=13$).
The number of equivalence relations on an $n$-set is the Bell number $B_n$ ($B_3=5$, $B_4=15$).
Every element in a component must also get its reflexive pair, including elements that appear in no pair of $R$.

questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,5,7,10,11\}$. The number of non-empty subsets of $S$ that have the sum of all elements a multiple of $3$, is ______. [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: Sort the elements by remainder mod $3$ (one of type $3k$, three of type $3k+1$, three of type $3k+2$) and count by size.
solution: Remainders mod $3$: $3k$ type: $\{3\}$ (one element); $3k+1$ type: $\{1,7,10\}$ (three); $3k+2$ type: $\{2,5,11\}$ (three).
$1$ element: the single set of type $3k$, so $1$ subset.
$2$ elements: one of type $3k+1$ and one of type $3k+2$: $3\times3=9$ subsets.
$3$ elements: $\{3k,3k+1,3k+2\}$ one each: $9$; three of $3k+1$: $1$; three of $3k+2$: $1$. Total $11$.
$4$ elements: $3k$ with three of $3k+1$: $1$; $3k$ with three of $3k+2$: $1$; two of $3k+1$ and two of $3k+2$: $\binom32\binom32=9$. Total $11$.
$5$ elements: $3k$ with two of $3k+1$ and two of $3k+2$: $9$ subsets.
$6$ elements: three of $3k+1$ and three of $3k+2$: $1$. $7$ elements: the set itself (sum $39$): $1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Roots-of-unity filter: the number of subsets with sum $\equiv0\pmod3$ is $\frac13\sum_{k=0}^{2}\prod_i\left(1+\omega^{ka_i}\right)$.
solution: Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. The number of subsets (including empty) with sum $\equiv0\pmod3$ is $N=\frac13\left[\prod_i(1+1)+\prod_i(1+\omega^{a_i})+\prod_i(1+\omega^{2a_i})\right]$.
The first product is $2^7=128$.
Residues: one element $\equiv0$ gives factor $2$; three $\equiv1$ give $(1+\omega)^3$; three $\equiv2$ give $(1+\omega^2)^3$.
$1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $1+\omega^2=-\omega$, so $(1+\omega)^3=-1$ and $(1+\omega^2)^3=-1$. The product is $2\cdot(-1)(-1)=2$.
The third product ($\omega^2$ in place of $\omega$) is its conjugate, also $2$.
$N=\frac{128+2+2}{3}=44$, including the empty set. Removing it, the answer is $43$.

useful_results: Roots-of-unity filter: the number of subsets of $\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}$ with sum $\equiv0\pmod m$ is $\frac1m\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\prod_i(1+\omega^{ka_i})$ (empty set included); here $\frac{128+2+2}{3}=44$.
Elements divisible by $m$ never affect the residue: they contribute a free factor $2^{n_0}$. Here $2\times22=44$ where $22$ counts subsets of the six non-multiples of $3$ with sum $\equiv0$.
With $n_1$ elements of residue $1$ and $n_2$ of residue $2$, choose $i$ and $j$ with $i+2j\equiv0\pmod3$, i.e. $i\equiv j\pmod3$.
Always subtract the empty set when the question asks for non-empty subsets.

questions.question: Among the relations $S=\left\{(a,b): a,b\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\},\ 2+\frac{a}{b}>0\right\}$ and $T=\left\{(a,b): a,b\in\mathbb{R},\ a^2-b^2\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}$ : [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: Test symmetry by swapping $(a,b)\to(b,a)$; a single numerical counterexample kills symmetry of $S$.
solution: For $T$: if $(a,b)\in T$ then $a^2-b^2=I$ for some integer $I$.
Then $b^2-a^2=-I$ is also an integer, so $(b,a)\in T$. Hence $T$ is symmetric.
For $S$: $(a,b)\in S$ means $2+\frac ab>0$, i.e. $\frac ab>-2$.
If $(b,a)\in S$ were forced, we would need $2+\frac ba>0$ whenever $2+\frac ab>0$; but $2+\frac ba$ is not necessarily positive.
Counterexample: $a=2,\ b=-5$. Then $2+\frac ab=2-\frac25=\frac85>0$, so $(2,-5)\in S$.
But $2+\frac ba=2-\frac52=-\frac12<0$, so $(-5,2)\notin S$. Hence $S$ is not symmetric.
So $T$ is symmetric but $S$ is not: option (B) (the other options each claim $S$ symmetric, or $T$ non-transitive, which is false: $a^2-b^2,\,b^2-c^2\in\mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow a^2-c^2\in\mathbb{Z}$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF text for T is garbled ('a^2-b^2=-I' should read a^2-b^2 = I, an integer). Its step '2+a/b>0 => a/b>-2 => b/a<-1/2' is wrong (taking reciprocals of an inequality is invalid when a/b can be positive: then b/a>0). Replaced by the counterexample a=2,b=-5; conclusion (B) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate options: $T$ is transitive (sum of two integers), which kills (A) and (C); a numerical example shows $S$ is not symmetric, which kills (D).
solution: Transitivity of $T$: if $a^2-b^2\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $b^2-c^2\in\mathbb{Z}$, then $a^2-c^2=(a^2-b^2)+(b^2-c^2)\in\mathbb{Z}$. So $T$ is transitive.
Option (A) says $T$ is not transitive and option (C) says neither is transitive: both are false.
Option (D) needs $S$ symmetric. Take $(a,b)=(2,-5)$: $2+\frac{2}{-5}=\frac85>0$ so $(2,-5)\in S$.
But $(b,a)=(-5,2)$ gives $2+\frac{-5}{2}=-\frac12<0$, so $(-5,2)\notin S$; (D) is false.
Only (B) is left; it is also confirmed directly, since $b^2-a^2=-(a^2-b^2)\in\mathbb{Z}$ makes $T$ symmetric.

useful_results: A relation $x\sim y\iff f(x)-f(y)\in\mathbb{Z}$ (or $f(x)=f(y)$) is always reflexive, symmetric and transitive, i.e. an equivalence relation; here $f(x)=x^2$.
To disprove symmetry, one pair $(a,b)\in R$ with $(b,a)\notin R$ is enough; choose numbers making one expression positive and the other negative.
Reciprocals reverse an inequality only when both sides have the same sign: $\frac ab>-2$ does not imply $\frac ba<-\frac12$ (take $\frac ab=2$). Always split the sign cases.
Elimination: when options pair statements about two objects, settle the easy object first ($T$ here) and discard options.

questions.question: The number of $3$-digit numbers, that are divisible by $2$ or $3$ but not divisible by $7$, is __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2023]
questions.key_idea: Count $(2\text{ or }3)$ by inclusion-exclusion, then remove those also divisible by $7$ using the same method.
solution: Numbers divisible by $7$ and by ($2$ or $3$): $64+43-21=86$.
Required count $=600-86=514$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The condition repeats with period $42$: count it in one block of $42$ consecutive integers, then handle the remainder.
solution: Among any $42$ consecutive integers, exactly $42\cdot\frac13=14$ are coprime to $6$, so $28$ are divisible by $2$ or $3$.
Multiples of $7$ in the block are $7j$ for $6$ consecutive values of $j$; $7j$ is divisible by $2$ or $3$ exactly when $j$ is, i.e. $6-2=4$ of them.
So each block of $42$ has $28-4=24$ numbers divisible by $2$ or $3$ but not by $7$.
The $900$ three-digit numbers are $21$ blocks of $42$ ($100$ to $981$) plus the $18$ numbers $982$ to $999$; the blocks give $21\times24=504$.
In $982,\dots,999$: evens $982,984,\dots,998$ ($9$ numbers) and odd multiples of $3$: $987,993,999$ ($3$), total $12$; remove the multiples of $7$: $987$ and $994$. That leaves $10$.

useful_results: Number of multiples of $m$ in $[L,U]$ is $\lfloor U/m\rfloor-\lfloor (L-1)/m\rfloor$. For three-digit numbers: $m=2:450$, $3:300$, $6:150$, $14:64$, $21:43$, $42:21$.
Three sets: $|P\cup Q\cup R|=\sum|P|-\sum|P\cap Q|+|P\cap Q\cap R|$; for multiples, $|P\cap Q|$ is the multiples of the LCM.
Divisibility conditions by $m_1,m_2,\dots$ repeat with period $\operatorname{lcm}(m_i)$; here the period is $42$, with $28$ numbers divisible by $2$ or $3$ per period (density $\frac23$).
'A but not B' $=|A|-|A\cap B|$; here $A$ = divisible by $2$ or $3$, $B$ = divisible by $7$.

questions.question: Let the number of elements in sets $A$ and $B$ be five and two respectively. Then the number of subsets of $A\times B$ each having at least $3$ and at most $6$ elements is : [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: $n(A\times B)=10$, so the required count is $\sum_{k=3}^{6}\binom{10}{k}$.
solution: $n(A)=5$ and $n(B)=2$, so $n(A\times B)=5\times2=10$.
A subset of $A\times B$ is any subset of this $10$-element set; we need those with $3,4,5$ or $6$ elements.
Number of such subsets $=\binom{10}{3}+\binom{10}{4}+\binom{10}{5}+\binom{10}{6}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complementary counting: remove subsets of size $0,1,2$ and $7$ to $10$ from all $2^{10}$ subsets, using $\binom{10}{k}=\binom{10}{10-k}$.
solution: All subsets of the $10$-element set: $2^{10}=1024$.

useful_results: $n(A\times B)=n(A)\,n(B)$, and a set with $m$ elements has $2^m$ subsets, $\binom mk$ of size $k$.
$\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk=2^n$; for a window of sizes use the complement when the window is large (here $1024-56-176$).
Number of relations from $A$ to $B$ is $2^{n(A)n(B)}$ (here $2^{10}$); 'subsets of $A\times B$' and 'relations from $A$ to $B$' are the same thing.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$. Then the relation $R=\{(x,y)\in A\times A: x+y=7\}$ is : [JEE(Main) April 2023]
options: transitive but neither symmetric nor reflexive
symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
questions.answer: (B) symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
questions.key_idea: List $R$ and test the three properties; $(1,6),(6,1)\in R$ but $(1,1)\notin R$ breaks both reflexivity and transitivity.
solution: Reflexive? $(1,1)\notin R$ since $1+1\ne7$. So $R$ is not reflexive.
Symmetric? Whenever $x+y=7$ we have $y+x=7$, so $(y,x)\in R$. Each listed pair has its reverse. $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive? $(1,6)\in R$ and $(6,1)\in R$ but $(1,1)\notin R$. So $R$ is not transitive.
Hence $R$ is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive: option (B). It is not an equivalence relation.
useful_results: $R=\{(x,y):x+y=c\}$ is always symmetric; it is reflexive only if $2x=c$ for every $x\in A$, which fails once $A$ has an element $\ne c/2$.
A symmetric relation with some $(x,y)\in R$ is transitive only if $(x,x)\in R$ (since $(x,y),(y,x)\in R$). One such failing pair disproves transitivity.
Equivalence relation = reflexive + symmetric + transitive; check the cheapest failing property first (reflexivity: one missing $(x,x)$).

questions.question: Let $A=\{2,3,4\}$ and $B=\{8,9,12\}$. Then the number of elements in the relation $R=\{((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2))\in(A\times B,\,A\times B): a_1\text{ divides }b_2\text{ and }a_2\text{ divides }b_1\}$ is : [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: The two divisibility conditions involve the separate pairs $(a_1,b_2)$ and $(a_2,b_1)$, so the count is the square of the number of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\mid b$.
solution: $a_1\in A$, $b_2\in B$ and $a_1$ divides $b_2$.
Similarly $a_2\in A$, $b_1\in B$ and $a_2$ divides $b_1$: the pairs $(a_2,b_1)$ are the same $6$ pairs.
The choice of $(a_1,b_2)$ and of $(a_2,b_1)$ is independent, and together they determine $((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2))$ uniquely.
Number of elements of $R=6\times6=36$.
questions.correction_note: PDF lists the first pair as (2,4), but 4 is not in B={8,9,12}; it should be (2,8). The count (6 pairs, 36) and the answer D are unchanged.
useful_results: For $a_1\mid b_2$ and $a_2\mid b_1$ the variables $(a_1,b_2)$ and $(a_2,b_1)$ are disjoint, so the count of $R$ is $N^2$ where $N=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a\mid b\}$.
$N=\sum_{a\in A}\#\{\text{multiples of }a\text{ in }B\}$; here $2\to\{8,12\}$, $3\to\{9,12\}$, $4\to\{8,12\}$, so $N=6$.
A relation on $A\times B$ is a set of pairs of ordered pairs: its universe has $(|A||B|)^2=81$ elements, so the answer must be at most $81$ (sanity bound).

concepts: Venn diagrams and set operations (3-set problems)
questions.question: An organization awarded $48$ medals in event 'A', $25$ in event 'B' and $18$ in event 'C'. If these medals went to total $60$ men and only five men got medals in all the three events, then, how many received medals in exactly two of three events : [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Let $x,y,z$ be the men with exactly two events and fill the three-circle Venn diagram; the total $60$ gives $x+y+z$.
solution: Let $x$ = men with medals in A and B only, $y$ = in B and C only, $z$ = in A and C only. Five men are in all three.
Sum of all regions equals the $60$ men: $(20-x-y)+(43-x-z)+(13-y-z)+x+y+z+5=60$.
Simplify: $81-(x+y+z)=60$.
Hence $x+y+z=21$: $21$ men received medals in exactly two events.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count medals by multiplicity: total medals $=n_1+2n_2+3n_3$ and total men $=n_1+n_2+n_3$.
solution: Let $n_1,n_2,n_3$ be the numbers of men with medals in exactly one, two, three events; $n_3=5$.
Counting men: $n_1+n_2+n_3=60$, so $n_1+n_2=55$.
Counting event-medals (each man counted once per event): $48+25+18=91=n_1+2n_2+3n_3$, so $n_1+2n_2=91-15=76$.

useful_results: $|A\cup B\cup C|=\sum|A|-\sum|A\cap B|+|A\cap B\cap C|$, and $\sum|A|=n_1+2n_2+3n_3$ where $n_k$ counts elements lying in exactly $k$ sets.
Exactly two sets: $n_2=\sum|A\cap B|-3|A\cap B\cap C|$ (here $36-15=21$, with $\sum|A\cap B|=x+y+z+3(5)=36$).
In a Venn diagram, 'only A' $=|A|-|A\cap B|-|A\cap C|+|A\cap B\cap C|$; fill the centre first, then the pairwise regions.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,3,4,6,9\}$ and $B=\{2,4,5,8,10\}$. Let $R$ be a relation defined on $A\times B$ such that $R=\{((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2)): a_1\le b_2\text{ and }b_1\le a_2\}$. Then the number of elements in the set $R$ is : [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: The conditions $a_1\le b_2$ and $b_1\le a_2$ involve separate coordinate pairs, so $|R|=N_1\cdot N_2$.
solution: The condition $a_1\le b_2$ restricts only $(a_1,b_2)$, and $b_1\le a_2$ restricts only $(a_2,b_1)$; the two choices are independent.
Number of elements of $R=16\times10=160$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Get $N_2$ from $N_1$ by complement: pairs with $a>b$ and pairs with $a\le b$ partition $A\times B$, and $N_2$ is $a>b$ plus $a=b$.
solution: Among the $5\times5=25$ pairs $(a,b)$, those with $a\le b$ number $N_1=16$ (counted by rows $5,4,4,2,1$).
So pairs with $a>b$ number $25-16=9$.
$N_2$ counts pairs with $b\le a$, i.e. $a>b$ plus $a=b$; $A\cap B=\{4\}$ gives one equal pair. So $N_2=9+1=10$.

useful_results: When a relation on $A\times B$ is defined by conditions on disjoint coordinate pairs, the count is the product of the two single-condition counts.
For finite sets: $\#\{a\le b\}+\#\{a>b\}=|A||B|$ and $\#\{a\ge b\}=\#\{a>b\}+|A\cap B|$, so $N_1+N_2=|A||B|+|A\cap B|=26$ here ($16+10$).
List by the variable with the fewest values first and count the allowed partners row-by-row; confirm with the sum rule $N_1+N_2=26$.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4,\dots,10\}$ and $B=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$. The number of elements in the relation $R=\{(a,b)\in A\times A: 2(a-b)^2+3(a-b)\in B\}$ is __________. [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Put $d=a-b$ and factor $2d^2+3d=d(2d+3)$; only integers $d=0$ and $d=-2$ give a value in $B$.
solution: Let $d=a-b$, an integer with $|d|\le9$. Then $2d^2+3d=d(2d+3)$.
It is $0$ iff $d=0$ (the other root $-\frac32$ is not an integer). Check $d=-2$: $(-2)(-1)=2\in B$.
Other integers: $d=1\to5$, $d=-1\to-1$, $d=-3\to9$, $d=2\to14$; for $d\ge1$ or $d\le-3$ the value is $\ge5$, so only $d=0,-2$ work.
So $a=b$ or $a-b=-2$.
When $a=b$: $10$ ordered pairs.
When $a-b=-2$, i.e. $b=a+2$ with $a=1,\dots,8$: $8$ ordered pairs.

alternate_solutions.idea: Go through each target value $k\in B$ and solve $2d^2+3d=k$; the discriminant $9+8k$ must be a perfect square for $d$ to be rational.
solution: Only $9$ and $25$ are perfect squares, so only $k=0$ and $k=2$ can give rational $d$.
$k=0$: $d=0$ or $d=-\frac32$; $k=2$: $d=\frac{-3\pm5}{4}=\frac12$ or $-2$. Integer values: $d=0,-2$.
Ordered pairs with $a-b=d$ in $\{1..10\}$ number $10-|d|$: $10$ for $d=0$ and $8$ for $d=-2$. Total $18$.

useful_results: In $\{1,\dots,n\}$, the number of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a-b=d$ is $n-|d|$ (here $n=10$: $10$ and $8$).
If a relation depends only on $d=a-b$, solve for admissible integer $d$ first, then count with $n-|d|$ and add over all admissible $d$.
$ax^2+bx+c=k$ has a rational root only if $b^2-4a(c-k)$ is a perfect square - a quick filter for integer candidates.

questions.question: Let $A=\{0,3,4,6,7,8,9,10\}$ and $R$ be the relation defined on $A$ such that $R=\{(x,y)\in A\times A: x-y\text{ is odd positive integer or }x-y=2\}$. The minimum number of elements that must be added to the relation $R$, so that it is a symmetric relation, is equal to __________. [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Every pair in $R$ has $x>y$, so no reverse pair is present; the number to add equals $|R|$.
solution: Arrange $A=\{10,9,8,7,6,4,3,0\}$ and list the pairs with $x-y$ odd positive or $x-y=2$.
Count the listed elements: $4+5+3+3+2+1+1=19$, so $|R|=19$.
Every element $(a,b)$ of $R$ has $a>b$ (because $x-y>0$ in both conditions).
Hence no reverse pair $(b,a)$ is in $R$, and for $R$ to be symmetric each of the $19$ reverses must be added.
The minimum number of elements to add is $19$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count $|R|$ without listing: opposite-parity pairs give the odd differences (one ordered pair each), plus the difference-$2$ pairs.
solution: $A$ has $5$ even elements $\{0,4,6,8,10\}$ and $3$ odd elements $\{3,7,9\}$.
$x-y$ is odd exactly when $x,y$ have opposite parity; each of the $5\times3=15$ such unordered pairs gives exactly one ordered pair with $x>y$. So $15$ pairs with odd positive difference.
Pairs with $x-y=2$: $(10,8),(9,7),(8,6),(6,4)$ (no other consecutive-by-2 elements, e.g. $4,2$ and $3,1$ are missing from $A$): $4$ pairs, all with even difference so none repeat.
$|R|=15+4=19$; since all pairs have $x>y$, the reverses are all new, so $19$ elements must be added.

useful_results: Minimum elements to add to make $R$ symmetric $=\#\{(x,y)\in R:(y,x)\notin R\}$ (the reverses missing from $R$); if $R$ has no symmetric pair this is $|R|$.
A relation defined by a strict inequality on a difference ($x-y>0$) is antisymmetric with no diagonal pairs, so none of its pairs is its own reverse.
$x-y$ odd $\iff$ $x,y$ have opposite parity; with $e$ evens and $o$ odds there are $e\cdot o$ unordered such pairs.

questions.question: The number of relations, on the set $\{1,2,3\}$ containing $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$, which are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is __________. [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Reflexive and transitive containing $(1,2),(2,3)$ forces $(1,3)$; then analyse which of the reverse pairs $(2,1),(3,2),(3,1)$ can be added without forcing symmetry.
solution: Transitive: $(1,2),(2,3)\in R\Rightarrow(1,3)\in R$.
Not symmetric: at least one of $(2,1),(3,2),(3,1)$ must be missing (if all three are present, $R$ is the full relation, which is symmetric). The extra pairs allowed are examined below.

Any relation containing $(3,1)$ must also contain $(3,2)$ (from $(3,1),(1,2)$) and $(2,1)$ (from $(2,3),(3,1)$), so it is the full relation, which is symmetric. Likewise $(2,1)$ together with $(3,2)$ forces $(3,1)$, i.e. full.
So exactly three relations qualify: $R_1,R_2,R_3$. Answer $3$ (the printed key '4' is wrong; the PDF itself lists only three relations).
questions.correction_note: PDF lists R1, R2, R3 (three relations) but then states the answer 4. Brute force over all 512 relations on {1,2,3} gives exactly 3 (R1, R1+(2,1), R1+(3,2)); adding (3,1) or both (2,1),(3,2) forces the full (symmetric) relation. The printed key 4 appears wrong; correct answer is 3.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat the three possible extra pairs $u=(2,1)$, $v=(3,2)$, $w=(3,1)$ as switches and list the implications forced by transitivity.
solution: Every valid $R$ contains the six pairs $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)$; the only freedom is which of $u,v,w$ are added.
Transitivity gives: $w=(3,1)$ with $(1,2)$ forces $v=(3,2)$; $w$ with $(2,3)$ forces $u=(2,1)$; $u$ with $v$ forces $w$ (since $(3,2),(2,1)\to(3,1)$).
Check transitivity of the first three directly; the last is the full relation $\{1,2,3\}^2$, which is symmetric and excluded.
Hence $3$ relations.

useful_results: Reflexive and transitive relations are preorders; on $3$ labelled points there are $29$ of them, $5$ of which are equivalence relations (Bell number $B_3=5$).
In a transitive relation, $(x,y),(y,x)\in R$ forces $(x,x)\in R$; with a chain $x\to y\to z$, a reverse arc $z\to x$ collapses all three into one class.
To count relations with given properties on a small set, fix the forced pairs first, then treat the remaining pairs as switches and list their implications.
Always cross-check an answer with the list actually written down; here the PDF's own list has three members.

concepts: Types of relations (reflexive and symmetric closure)
questions.question: Let $A=\{-4,-3,-2,0,1,3,4\}$ and $R=\{(a,b)\in A\times A: b=|a|\text{ or }b^2=a+1\}$ be a relation on $A$. Then the minimum number of elements, that must be added to the relation $R$ so that it becomes reflexive and symmetric, is __________. [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Write $R$ explicitly (checking each root $b=\pm\sqrt{a+1}$ lies in $A$), then count missing diagonal pairs and missing reverses.
solution: $b^2=a+1$: $a=0\Rightarrow b=\pm1$, only $b=1\in A$: $(0,1)$. $a=3\Rightarrow b=\pm2$, only $b=-2\in A$: $(3,-2)$. Other $a$ give $b^2<0$ or non-integer $b$.
Symmetric: reverses of $(-4,4),(-3,3),(3,-2),(0,1)$ are missing; add $(4,-4),(3,-3),(-2,3),(1,0)$. Add $4$ elements.
The pairs added for reflexivity are diagonal and need no reverse, so the two sets of additions are disjoint.
Minimum number to add $=3+4=7$.
useful_results: Minimum additions to make $R$ reflexive and symmetric $=\#\{x:(x,x)\notin R\}+\#\{\text{unordered pairs }\{x,y\},x\ne y,\text{ with exactly one of }(x,y),(y,x)\in R\}$.
Adding diagonal pairs never creates a new reverse requirement, so the two counts can be added.
For conditions like $b^2=a+1$ solve $b=\pm\sqrt{a+1}$ and keep only roots that lie in the given set; for $b=|a|$ keep only $a$ with $|a|\in A$.
Each off-diagonal pair already present in both directions needs nothing; here none of the $4$ off-diagonal pairs has its reverse.

concepts: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $R$ be a relation on the set $A\times A$ defined by $R=\{((a,b),(c,d)):2a+3b=4c+5d\}$. Then the number of elements in $R$ is _________. [JEE(Main) April 2023]
questions.key_idea: Tabulate $2a+3b$ and $4c+5d$ and add up (number of $(a,b)$ with value $\alpha$) $\times$ (number of $(c,d)$ with value $\alpha$).
solution: $R$ consists of pairs $((a,b),(c,d))$ with $a,b,c,d\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $2a+3b=4c+5d$. Call the common value $\alpha$.
The values common to both tables are $\alpha=9,13,14,14,17,18$ (the PDF lists $14$ twice because $2a+3b=14$ happens for two pairs).
$\alpha=9$: $(a,b)=(3,1)$ and $(c,d)=(1,1)$, giving $1$ element of $R$. $\alpha=13$: $(2,3)$ and $(2,1)$, giving $1$.
$\alpha=14$: $(a,b)=(1,4)$ or $(4,2)$ and $(c,d)=(1,2)$, giving $2$ elements.
Hence the number of elements of $R$ is $1+1+2+1+1=6$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce modulo $2$: $b\equiv d \pmod 2$, then $a=2c+\frac{5d-3b}{2}$ must lie in $\{1,2,3,4\}$, so only $8$ pairs $(b,d)$ need checking.
solution: $2a$ and $4c$ are even, so $3b-5d=4c-2a$ is even; hence $b\equiv d\pmod 2$.
Then $a=2c+k$ with $k=\frac{5d-3b}{2}$ an integer; for each $(b,d)$ with $b\equiv d$ count the $c\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ with $1\le 2c+k\le 4$.
$k=2$ gives $c=1$ ($a=4$): 1 solution; $k=-1$ gives $c=1,2$ ($a=1,3$): 2 solutions; $k=7$ and $k=4$ give none.
Total $1+2+1+2=6$, the same count.

useful_results: Counting pairs with equal values: $\#\{(u,v):f(u)=g(v)\}=\sum_\alpha N_f(\alpha)\,N_g(\alpha)$; here $1+1+2+1+1=6$.
A relation on $A\times A$ is a subset of $(A\times A)\times(A\times A)$, so it has up to $|A|^4=256$ possible elements here.
Parity first: in $2a+3b=4c+5d$ the parity of $3b-5d$ forces $b\equiv d \pmod 2$, halving the search space.
Quick range check: $2a+3b\in[5,20]$ and $4c+5d\in[9,36]$, so only $\alpha\in[9,20]$ can occur.

concepts: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive relations on a power set
questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,10\}$. Suppose $M$ is the set of all the subsets of $S$, then the relation $R=\{(A,B):A\cap B\neq\phi;\ A,B\in M\}$ is: [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: The empty set $\phi\in M$ is not related to itself, which kills reflexivity; sharing an element is symmetric but not transitive.
solution: $R=\{(A,B):A\cap B\neq\phi;\ A,B\in M\}$, where $M$ is the set of all subsets of $S$.
Reflexive: $M$ consists of subsets of $S$, so $\phi\in M$. For $A=\phi$ we get $\phi\cap\phi=\phi$, but $R$ needs $A\cap B\neq\phi$. So $(\phi,\phi)\notin R$ and $R$ is not reflexive.
Symmetric: if $ARB$ then $A\cap B\neq\phi$.
Since $B\cap A=A\cap B\neq\phi$, we get $BRA$. So $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive: take $A=\{1,2\}$, $B=\{2,3\}$, $C=\{3,4\}$, all subsets of $S$ (the PDF used sets of ordered pairs, which are not subsets of $S$).
$A\cap B=\{2\}\neq\phi$ and $B\cap C=\{3\}\neq\phi$, so $ARB$ and $BRC$, but $A\cap C=\phi$, so $A$ is not related to $C$. Not transitive.
So $R$ is symmetric only, option (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote 'B∩A ∈ φ' (typo for ≠ φ) and gave the transitivity counterexample with sets of ordered pairs such as A={(1,2),(2,3)}, which are not subsets of S. Replaced by genuine subsets A={1,2}, B={2,3}, C={3,4}; the conclusion (A) is unchanged.
useful_results: On the power set, $A\cap B\neq\phi$ is symmetric always; reflexive on non-empty sets only (fails exactly at $\phi$); transitive fails whenever $|S|\ge2$ (e.g. $\{1\},\{1,2\},\{2\}$).
First test every property on the 'special' element ($\phi$, $0$, the identity) - it is where reflexivity usually breaks.
To refute transitivity, find a chain $A\to B\to C$ with $A,C$ unrelated; for 'overlap' relations take three sets overlapping consecutively but not end to end.
A relation that is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive must have an element related to nothing (here $\phi$).

concepts: Number of subsets of a finite set
questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be two finite sets with $m$ and $n$ elements respectively. The total number of subsets of the set $A$ is $56$ more than the total number of subsets of $B$. Then the distance of the point $P(m,n)$ from the point $Q(-2,-3)$ is: [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: Subset counts are $2^m$ and $2^n$, so the condition is $2^m-2^n=56=64-8$.
solution: A set with $k$ elements has $2^k$ subsets, so $A$ has $2^m$ subsets and $B$ has $2^n$ subsets.
Since $56=64-8=2^6-2^3$, we get $m=6$ and $n=3$ (uniqueness is shown in the alternate method).

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor $2^m-2^n=2^n(2^{m-n}-1)$: the bracket is odd, so $2^n$ is exactly the power of $2$ in $56$.
solution: Since $2^m-2^n=56>0$, $m>n$, and $2^m-2^n=2^n\left(2^{m-n}-1\right)$.
$2^{m-n}-1$ is odd (as $m-n\ge1$), so $2^n$ is the highest power of $2$ dividing $56=2^3\cdot7$. Hence $n=3$.
Then $2^{m-n}-1=7$, so $2^{m-n}=8$ and $m-n=3$, giving $m=6$. This is the only solution.

useful_results: A finite set with $k$ elements has $2^k$ subsets, $2^k-1$ non-empty and $2^k-1$ proper subsets.
$2^m-2^n=2^n(2^{m-n}-1)$ with an odd bracket: the 2-adic part of the right side identifies $n$ uniquely (check: $2^6-2^3=8\cdot7=56$).
Distance between $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is $\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}$; $8,6,10$ is a $3$-$4$-$5$ triple, which can be spotted at once.

questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $(a,b)R(c,d)$ if and only if $ad-bc$ is divisible by $5$. Then $R$ is: [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
options: Reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.answer: (B) Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.key_idea: The pair $(0,0)$ (or a non-proportional pair of vectors mod $5$) gives a quick counterexample to transitivity.
solution: Reflexive: $(a,b)R(a,b)$ because $ab-ba=0$ is divisible by $5$. So $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: let $(a,b)R(c,d)$, i.e. $ad-bc$ is divisible by $5$.
Then $bc-ad=-(ad-bc)$ is also divisible by $5$, so $(c,d)R(a,b)$. So $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive: $(3,1)R(10,5)$ since $3\cdot5-1\cdot10=5$ is divisible by $5$.
$(10,5)R(1,1)$ since $10\cdot1-5\cdot1=5$ is divisible by $5$.
But $(3,1)R(1,1)$ would need $3\cdot1-1\cdot1=2$ divisible by $5$, which is false. So $R$ is not transitive.
Hence $R$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $ad-bc\equiv0\pmod5$ as 'the vectors $(a,b)$, $(c,d)$ are dependent mod $5$'; the zero vector is related to everything.
solution: $ad-bc$ is the determinant of the vectors $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$; $R$ says the determinant is $0 \pmod 5$ (the two vectors are linearly dependent over $\mathbb{Z}_5$).
A vector is dependent with itself (determinant $0$) and the determinant changes sign on swapping, so $R$ is reflexive and symmetric.
The zero vector $(0,0)$ has determinant $0$ with every vector, so $(1,0)R(0,0)$ and $(0,0)R(0,1)$.
But $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ have determinant $1\cdot1-0\cdot0=1$, not divisible by $5$, so $(1,0)$ is not related to $(0,1)$. Transitivity fails; the answer is (B).

useful_results: '$ad-bc\equiv0$' relations (proportionality of pairs) become transitive if the zero pair is excluded: on non-zero pairs over a field it is an equivalence relation (classes are lines through $0$). Over $\mathbb{Z}_5$ this is exactly where $(0,0)$ is the only spoiler.
A quick transitivity counterexample: use a 'universal' element (zero vector, empty set, $0$) that is related to everything.
Symmetry of a relation defined by a skew expression $f(x,y)=-f(y,x)$ with condition $f=0$ (or $f\equiv0$ mod $m$) is automatic.
A relation defined by $g(x)=g(y)$ is always an equivalence; one defined by $f(x,y)\equiv0$ with a determinant-type $f$ is not, in general.

concepts: Smallest equivalence relation containing given pairs
questions.question: If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $\{(1,2),(1,3)\}\subset R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: Closing $\{(1,2),(1,3)\}$ under reflexive, symmetric and transitive rules merges $1,2,3$ into one class and leaves $\{4\}$ alone.
solution: For reflexivity $R$ must contain $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)$.
For symmetry, $(1,2)$ requires $(2,1)$ and $(1,3)$ requires $(3,1)$.
Since $(2,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are in $R$, transitivity requires $(2,3)$; similarly $(3,1)$ and $(1,2)$ require $(3,2)$.
Hence $R$ must have minimum $10$ elements.

alternate_solutions.idea: An equivalence relation is a partition into classes; the smallest one containing the pairs has classes $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{4\}$.
solution: $1\sim2$ and $1\sim3$ force $1,2,3$ into one class; nothing links $4$, so the smallest equivalence relation has classes $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{4\}$.
A class of size $k$ contributes $k^2$ ordered pairs: $3^2+1^2=10$.

useful_results: Equivalence relations on $A$ correspond to partitions of $A$; a class of size $k$ contributes $k^2$ ordered pairs, so $|R|=\sum k_i^2$ (here $9+1=10$).
The smallest equivalence relation containing given pairs: join elements connected through the pairs (connected components of the graph); each component is one class.
Number of equivalence relations on an $n$-set is the Bell number: $1,2,5,15,52$ for $n=1,\dots,5$.
Size of an equivalence relation on $n$ elements lies between $n$ (identity) and $n^2$ (universal).

questions.question: Consider the relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ defined as $aR_1b\iff a^2+b^2=1$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $(a,b)R_2(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c$ for all $(a,b),(c,d)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Then: [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
options: Neither $R_1$ nor $R_2$ is an equivalence relation
questions.key_idea: $R_1$ fails reflexivity ($a^2+a^2=1$ is false for $a=0$); $R_2$ says $a-b=c-d$, which is automatically an equivalence.
solution: $R_1=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}:a^2+b^2=1\}$. It is not reflexive, since $(0,0)\notin R_1$ ($0+0\neq1$). So $R_1$ is not an equivalence relation.
$R_2$: $(a,b)R_2(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c$. Reflexive: $(a,b)R_2(a,b)\iff a+b=b+a$, true.
Symmetric: $(a,b)R_2(c,d)\Rightarrow a+d=b+c\Rightarrow d+a=c+b\Rightarrow c+b=d+a\Rightarrow(c,d)R_2(a,b)$, true.
Transitive: $(a,b)R_2(c,d)\Rightarrow a+d=b+c$ (1) and $(c,d)R_2(e,f)\Rightarrow c+f=d+e$ (2).
Adding (1) and (2): $a+d+c+f=b+c+d+e$, so $a+f=b+e$, i.e. $(a,b)R_2(e,f)$. Transitive.
So $R_2$ is an equivalence relation and $R_1$ is not: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: $a+d=b+c\iff a-b=c-d$: $R_2$ relates pairs having the same value of $f(a,b)=a-b$, so it is an equivalence automatically.
solution: $(a,b)R_2(c,d)\iff a-b=c-d$, i.e. $f(a,b)=f(c,d)$ for $f(a,b)=a-b$.
'Same value of a function' is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so $R_2$ is an equivalence relation; its classes are the diagonals $a-b=\text{const}$.
$R_1$ is not reflexive because $a^2+a^2=1$ fails at $a=0$. Hence only $R_2$ is an equivalence relation: (C).

useful_results: Any relation of the form $xRy\iff f(x)=f(y)$ is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the level sets of $f$.
A relation like $a^2+b^2=1$ (a 'locus' relation) is never reflexive on all of $\mathbb{R}$; test one point, e.g. $a=0$.
To spot a hidden $f(x)=f(y)$: rearrange $a+d=b+c$ to $a-b=c-d$ (check: $(5,2)$ and $(4,1)$ are related, both have difference $3$).
Reflexive and transitive proofs for such relations are usually one line of algebra; symmetric uses $f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow f(y)=f(x)$.

concepts: Sets of ordered pairs defined by an equation
questions.question: Let the set $C=\{(x,y)\mid x^2-2^y=2023,\ x,y\in\mathbb{N}\}$. Then $\sum_{(x,y)\in C}(x+y)$ is equal to __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: For $y\ge2$, $x^2\equiv2023\equiv3\pmod 4$ is impossible, so $y=1$ and $x=45$ is the only element of $C$.
solution: $x^2-2^y=2023$ with $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$.
Added (uniqueness): if $y\ge2$ then $2^y\equiv0\pmod4$, so $x^2\equiv2023\equiv3\pmod4$, impossible because squares are $0$ or $1 \pmod 4$. So $y=1$.
Therefore $\sum_{(x,y)\in C}(x+y)=45+1=46$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF only states 'x=45, y=1' and sums to 46; it gives no argument that this is the only element of C. The answer is right; the mod-4 uniqueness step was added (and $y=0$ if $0\in\mathbb{N}$ gives $x^2=2024$, not a square).
useful_results: Squares are $0$ or $1\pmod4$ (and $0,1,4\pmod8$): use this to cut down equations $x^2-2^y=k$ immediately.
For $k\equiv3\pmod4$, $x^2-2^y=k$ has no solution with $y\ge2$; only $y=0,1$ need checking (check: $45^2-2=2023$).
When a question says 'sum over all elements of the set', first establish how many elements the set has - here exactly one.

concepts: Venn diagrams and inclusion-exclusion for three sets
questions.question: A group of $40$ students appeared in an examination of $3$ subjects - Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry. It was found that all students passed in at least one of the subjects, $20$ students passed in Mathematics, $25$ students passed in Physics, $16$ students passed in Chemistry, at most $11$ students passed in both Mathematics and Physics, at most $15$ students passed in both Physics and Chemistry, at most $15$ students passed in both Mathematics and Chemistry. The maximum number of students passed in all three subjects is __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: Check an upper bound $x\le11$ against the other data; $x=11$ is infeasible, $x=10$ is realised by an explicit Venn diagram.
solution: Let $x$ students pass all three subjects (centre of the Venn diagram). The region 'Maths and Physics only' has $|M\cap P|-x\ge0$ students, and $|M\cap P|\le11$, so $11-x\ge0$, i.e. $x\le11$.
Test $x=11$: then $|M\cap P|=11$. Inclusion-exclusion gives $40=20+25+16-(11+|P\cap C|+|M\cap C|)+11$, so $|P\cap C|+|M\cap C|=21$.
But each of $|P\cap C|,|M\cap C|$ is at least $x=11$, so their sum is at least $22$, a contradiction. So $x=11$ does not satisfy the data.
Try $x=10$ with regions: $M$ only $9$, $P$ only $15$, $C$ only $5$, $M\&P$ only $0$, $P\&C$ only $0$, $M\&C$ only $1$, all three $10$.
Pair limits: $|M\cap P|=10\le11$, $|P\cap C|=10\le15$, $|M\cap C|=11\le15$. All satisfied.
Hence the maximum number of students passing all three subjects is $10$ (the printed key $11$ is wrong; NTA key is $10$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's printed 'Ans. 11' is wrong: its own working rejects x=11 and gets x=10, and a brute-force check confirms the maximum is 10 (the PDF itself notes 'Matrix answer NTA (10)'). Added the justification why x=11 fails; the working was otherwise kept.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count subject-incidences: $61=n_1+2n_2+3x$ with $n_1+n_2+x=40$ gives $n_2=21-2x\ge0$, so $x\le10$ at once.
solution: Let $n_1,n_2,x$ be the numbers of students passing exactly one, exactly two, all three subjects. Everyone passes at least one: $n_1+n_2+x=40$.
Counting passes by subject: $20+25+16=61=n_1+2n_2+3x$.
Subtract: $61-40=n_2+2x$, so $n_2=21-2x\ge0$, giving $x\le10.5$, i.e. $x\le10$ (for integers).
$x=10$ is attainable (e.g. $n_2=1$ in the diagram: $9,15,5$ only-one regions and $1$ student in $M\cap C$ only), meeting every pair limit, so the maximum is $10$.

useful_results: Incidence counting: if $|A|+|B|+|C|=T$ and $n$ students lie in the union, then $T=n_1+2n_2+3n_3$ and $n=n_1+n_2+n_3$, so $T-n=n_2+2n_3$.
Inclusion-exclusion: $|A\cup B\cup C|=\sum|A|-\sum|A\cap B|+|A\cap B\cap C|$ (check here: $61-(10+10+11)+10=40$).
For maximum/minimum questions, get a bound, then always construct a case that attains it; do not just trust the bound.
Every pairwise intersection is at least $|A\cap B\cap C|$ and each 'only' region must be non-negative.

questions.question: The number of symmetric relations defined on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ which are not reflexive is __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: A symmetric relation on an $n$-set is fixed by $n(n+1)/2$ independent choices, and a reflexive one by $n(n-1)/2$.
solution: For a set with $n$ elements, the number of relations that are both symmetric and reflexive is $2^{\frac{n^2-n}{2}}$ (diagonal pairs forced in; one choice per unordered pair $\{i,j\}$, $i\neq j$).
The total number of symmetric relations is $2^{\frac{n^2+n}{2}}$ (one choice for each of the $\frac{n(n+1)}2$ unordered pairs, including diagonal ones).
Number of symmetric relations that are not reflexive $=2^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}-2^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes '(n = 5)' but then evaluates $2^{10}-2^6$, which is the value for $n=4$ (the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$); for $n=5$ the formula would give $2^{15}-2^{10}$. Only the label was wrong; the answer 960 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the choices: $6$ free off-diagonal pairs and $4$ diagonal pairs; 'not reflexive' means the diagonal is not all present.
solution: A symmetric relation is determined by which of the $6$ unordered pairs $\{i,j\}$ ($i\ne j$) are present: $2^6=64$ choices.
It is also determined by which of the $4$ diagonal pairs $(i,i)$ are present: $2^4=16$ choices.
Not reflexive means not all $4$ diagonal pairs are present: $16-1=15$ choices.
Total $=64\times15=960$.

useful_results: On an $n$-set: relations $2^{n^2}$; reflexive $2^{n^2-n}$; symmetric $2^{n(n+1)/2}$; reflexive and symmetric $2^{n(n-1)/2}$ (for $n=4$: $65536,4096,1024,64$).
Symmetric but not reflexive: $2^{n(n+1)/2}-2^{n(n-1)/2}=2^{n(n-1)/2}(2^n-1)$ (check $n=2$: $8-2=6=2\cdot3$).
Antisymmetric relations: $2^n\cdot3^{n(n-1)/2}$ (diagonal free, each off-diagonal pair has $3$ options).
Count by independent choices: diagonal entries and unordered off-diagonal pairs are independent for symmetric relations.

concepts: Smallest equivalence relation containing a given relation
questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $R=\{(1,2),(2,3),(1,4)\}$ be a relation on $A$. Let $S$ be the equivalence relation on $A$ such that $R\subset S$ and the number of elements in $S$ is $n$. Then, the minimum value of $n$ is __________. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: $1,2,3,4$ are all linked through $R$, so the smallest equivalence relation has a single class and is $A\times A$.
solution: Symmetric: add $(2,1)$, $(3,2)$, $(4,1)$ (the PDF lists $(3,1)$ here instead of $(3,2)$).
Now the relation has $(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(1,4),(4,1)$ besides the diagonal.
Transitive: $(1,2),(2,3)\Rightarrow(1,3)$ and so $(3,1)$; $(3,1),(1,4)\Rightarrow(3,4)$ and so $(4,3)$; $(2,1),(1,4)\Rightarrow(2,4)$ and so $(4,2)$.
So we add $(1,3),(3,1),(3,4),(4,3),(2,4),(4,2)$, which completes all of $A\times A$.
Total added $=4+3+6=13$ elements to $R$, which had $3$.
So the minimum number of elements in $S$ is $3+13=16$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's list of symmetric additions is '(2,1),(4,1),(3,1)': the symmetric partner of (2,3) is (3,2), not (3,1). With (3,1) listed again in the transitive step and (3,2) never added, the printed list is not a valid closure. Fixed to (2,1),(3,2),(4,1) and transitive additions (1,3),(3,1),(3,4),(4,3),(2,4),(4,2); the count 13 added and n=16 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Connectivity: $R$ links $1-2$, $2-3$, $1-4$, so all four elements lie in one class; one class means $S=A\times A$.
solution: The smallest equivalence relation containing $R$ identifies elements joined by a chain of pairs of $R$ (in either direction).
$1\sim2$, $2\sim3$, $1\sim4$ join all of $1,2,3,4$ into a single class.
One class of size $4$ gives $4^2=16$ ordered pairs, so $n_{\min}=16$.

useful_results: The smallest equivalence relation containing $R$ is given by the connected components of the graph of $R$ (ignoring direction); its size is $\sum k_i^2$ over component sizes $k_i$.
A connected graph on $n$ vertices forces $S=A\times A$ with $n^2$ elements ($n=4$: $16$).
Transitive closure of a symmetric relation is symmetric, so the order reflexive, symmetric, transitive needs no repeat.
Check on a case: $R=\{(1,2)\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ gives classes $\{1,2\},\{3\}$ and $4+1=5$ elements.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\ldots,100\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A$ defined by $(x,y)\in R$ if and only if $2x=3y$. Let $R_1$ be a symmetric relation on $A$ such that $R\subset R_1$ and the number of elements in $R_1$ is $n$. Then, the minimum value of $n$ is ______. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: A symmetric $R_1\supseteq R$ must contain every reverse pair $(y,x)$, so the minimum is $R\cup R^{-1}$.
solution: $2x=3y$ forces $x$ to be a multiple of $3$ and $y$ a multiple of $2$: $x=3k,\ y=2k$.
Both must lie in $A$, so $3k\le100$, i.e. $1\le k\le33$.
A symmetric $R_1$ containing $R$ must also contain $(2k,3k)$ for every $(3k,2k)\in R$.
None of these reverse pairs is in $R$: $(2k,3k)\in R$ would need $4k=9k$, impossible. Also $R$ has no pair $(x,x)$, since $2x=3x$ gives $x=0$.
So exactly $33$ new, distinct pairs are needed, and the minimum is $n=33+33=66$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The smallest symmetric relation containing $R$ is $R\cup R^{-1}$, so $n=2|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$.
solution: Any symmetric $R_1\supseteq R$ contains $R^{-1}$, and $R\cup R^{-1}$ is itself symmetric. Hence the minimum is $|R\cup R^{-1}|=|R|+|R^{-1}|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$.
$|R^{-1}|=|R|$, since $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$ is a bijection.
$(x,y)\in R\cap R^{-1}$ means $2x=3y$ and $2y=3x$. Subtracting the second from the first gives $5x=5y$, so $x=y$, and then $2x=3x$ forces $x=0\notin A$. So $R\cap R^{-1}=\emptyset$.

useful_results: Smallest symmetric relation containing $R$ is $R\cup R^{-1}$, of size $2|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$; its size is $2|R|$ when $R$ has no symmetric pair.

$R\cap R^{-1}$ is exactly the set of pairs $(x,y)$ with both $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$ in $R$; it includes every diagonal pair $(x,x)\in R$. Check: $R=\{(1,1),(1,2)\}$ gives $R\cup R^{-1}=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)\}$, size $2\cdot2-1=3$.
For $ax=by$ on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $a\ne b$: pairs are $(bk,ak)$ with $k\le\lfloor N/\max(a,b)\rfloor$; here $\lfloor100/3\rfloor=33$.

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\ldots,20\}$. Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be two relations on $A$ such that $R_1=\{(a,b)\}$ where $b$ is divisible by $a$, and $R_2=\{(a,b)\}$ where $a$ is an integral multiple of $b$. Then the number of elements in $R_1-R_2$ is equal to ______. [JEE(Main) Jan 2024]
questions.key_idea: $R_1\cap R_2$ is just the diagonal, so $|R_1-R_2|=|R_1|-20$.
solution: The number of pairs with first entry $a$ is $\lfloor 20/a\rfloor$: $20,10,6,5,4,3,2,2,2,2$ for $a=1,\ldots,10$ and $1$ for each of $a=11,\ldots,20$.
$R_2$: $(a,b)\in R_2$ iff $a$ is a multiple of $b$, i.e. $b\mid a$.
$(a,b)\in R_1\cap R_2$ needs $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$, so $a=b$: $R_1\cap R_2=\{(1,1),(2,2),\ldots,(20,20)\}$, which has $20$ pairs.
$R_1-R_2=R_1-(R_1\cap R_2)$, so the number of elements is $66-20=46$.
useful_results: $|\{(a,b): 1\le a,b\le N,\ a\mid b\}|=\sum_{a=1}^{N}\lfloor N/a\rfloor=\sum_{b=1}^{N}d(b)$, where $d(b)$ is the number of divisors of $b$. Check $N=4$: $4+2+1+1=8$ and $1+2+2+3=8$.
$a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$ (positive integers) imply $a=b$; so divisibility is antisymmetric and $R_1\cap R_2$ is the diagonal.
$R_2=R_1^{-1}$; so $R_1-R_2$ is the set of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\mid b$, $a\ne b$ (a proper-divisor pair), of size $\sum_{b\le N}(d(b)-1)$.

questions.question: Let a relation $R$ on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ be defined as $(x_1,y_1)\,R\,(x_2,y_2)$ if and only if $x_1\le x_2$ or $y_1\le y_2$. Consider the two statements: (I) $R$ is reflexive but not symmetric. (II) $R$ is transitive. Then which of the following is true? [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: To refute a property of a relation, one explicit counter-example is enough; for an 'or' relation choose pairs where both inequalities fail.
solution: Reflexive: $(5,4)\,R\,(5,4)$ because $5\le5$. In general $(x,y)R(x,y)$ as $x\le x$. So $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric? Take $(1,2)\,R\,(3,4)$: true, since $1\le3$ (or $2\le4$).
But $(3,4)\,R\,(1,2)$ needs $3\le1$ or $4\le2$, both false. So $(3,4)\not R\,(1,2)$ and $R$ is not symmetric. Hence (I) is correct.
Transitive? Take $(3,7)\,R\,(4,3)$: true since $3\le4$.
Also $(4,3)\,R\,(1,3)$: true since $3\le3$.
But $(3,7)\,R\,(1,3)$ needs $3\le1$ or $7\le3$, both false. So $(3,7)\not R\,(1,3)$ and $R$ is not transitive. Hence (II) is false.
Only (I) is correct: option (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes '(3,7)R(4,3) and (4,3)R(1,3) => (3,7)R(1,3)' and '(1,2)R(3,4) => (3,4)R(1,2)', which as printed are false implications (the intended arrows are 'does not imply', i.e. counter-examples); it never states the verdict on (II) explicitly. The counter-example pairs and answer (A) are right; corrected by showing the failing inequalities and stating that (II) is false.
useful_results: A relation defined with 'or' between coordinate inequalities is reflexive, and is non-transitive/non-symmetric in general: fail it by choosing pairs for which BOTH inequalities fail.
To disprove transitivity find $a\,R\,b$, $b\,R\,c$ with $a\not R\,c$; to disprove symmetry find $a\,R\,b$ with $b\not R\,a$. One example suffices; to prove a property you must argue for all elements.
The 'and' version ($x_1\le x_2$ and $y_1\le y_2$) is a partial order (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive), unlike this 'or' version.

questions.question: Let the relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ on the set $X=\{1,2,3,\ldots,20\}$ be given by $R_1=\{(x,y):2x-3y=2\}$ and $R_2=\{(x,y):-5x+4y=0\}$. If $M$ and $N$ are the minimum number of elements required to be added in $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, in order to make the relations symmetric, then $M+N$ equals: [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: Each pair of $R_1,R_2$ has a reverse that is not already present, so the number to add equals the size of each relation.
solution: For $R_1$: $2x-3y=2$ gives $y=\frac{2x-2}{3}$, so $x\equiv1\pmod3$ with $x,y\in X$.
$R_1=\{(4,2),(7,4),(10,6),(13,8),(16,10),(19,12)\}$, where $x=1$ is excluded since it gives $y=0\notin X$, and $x=19$ is the last value.
For $R_2$: $-5x+4y=0$ gives $y=\frac{5x}{4}$, so $x$ is a multiple of $4$.
For $R_1$ to be symmetric the reverse pairs $(2,4),(4,7),\ldots,(12,19)$ are needed; none of them satisfies $2x-3y=2$, so none is in $R_1$. Hence $6$ elements must be added: $M=6$.
Similarly the reverses $(5,4),(10,8),(15,12),(20,16)$ are not in $R_2$, so $N=4$.
useful_results: Minimum number to add for symmetry $=|R^{-1}\setminus R|$ $=\;|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$ (the number of pairs whose reverse is missing).
A line relation $ax+by=c$ on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is counted by finding the congruence class of $x$ and the range limit; verify the end values ($x=1$ and the last $x$) separately.

A pair $(x,y)$ of $ax=by$ type has its reverse in the relation only if $ay=bx$ too, which forces $x=y$ when $a\ne b$ (here $x=y=0$); so no pair is its own reverse partner. Check: $(4,5)\in R_2$ but $(5,4)$ gives $-25+16\ne0$.

questions.question: Let $A$ be the set of all $n\in[100,700]\cap\mathbb{N}$ such that $n$ is neither a multiple of $3$ nor a multiple of $4$. Then the number of elements in $A$ is: [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: Count multiples of $3$, $4$ and $12$ by A.P. term counts, then use $n(3\cup4)=n(3)+n(4)-n(3\cap4)$ and subtract from the total.
solution: The interval $[100,700]$ contains $700-100+1=601$ integers.
Multiples of both $3$ and $4$ (multiples of $12$): $108,120,\ldots,696$. From $696=108+(n-1)12$ we get $n=50$, so $n(3\cap4)=50$.
Numbers that are neither: $601-301=300$. Option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Divisibility by $3$ and $4$ repeats with period $12$, and exactly $6$ residues mod $12$ are free of both.
solution: Whether $n$ is a multiple of $3$ or $4$ depends only on $n \bmod 12$.
Residues $0,\ldots,11$ that are multiples of $3$ or $4$: $0,3,4,6,8,9$. The other $6$ residues, $1,2,5,7,10,11$, are good.
The block $100,\ldots,699$ has $600$ consecutive integers, which is exactly $50$ full periods of $12$, so it contains $50\times6=300$ good numbers.
The remaining number $700=12\cdot58+4$ is a multiple of $4$, so it is not good.
Total $=300$.

useful_results: Inclusion-exclusion: $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$; multiples of both $3$ and $4$ are the multiples of $\operatorname{lcm}=12$.
Number of multiples of $d$ in $[a,b]$ is $\lfloor b/d\rfloor-\lfloor (a-1)/d\rfloor$. Check: multiples of $3$ in $[100,700]$: $233-33=200$.
Over any $12$ consecutive integers, exactly $12(1-\frac13-\frac14+\frac1{12})=6$ are multiples of neither $3$ nor $4$ (residues $1,2,5,7,10,11$).

questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A$ defined by $xRy$ if and only if $4x\le5y$. Let $m$ be the number of elements in $R$ and $n$ be the minimum number of elements from $A\times A$ that are required to be added to $R$ to make it a symmetric relation. Then $m+n$ is equal to: [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: Count pairs with $4x\le5y$ row by row; the pairs to add are the reverses $(y,x)$ of pairs of $R$ that are not themselves in $R$.
solution: $xRy$ iff $y\ge\frac{4x}{5}$. For $x=1$: $y\ge0.8$, so $y=1,2,3,4,5$ ($5$ pairs).
Pairs of $R$ whose reverse is missing: all off-diagonal pairs except $(4,5),(5,4)$, which are already each other's reverse.
useful_results: $|R\cup R^{-1}|=2|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$; number to add $=|R|-|R\cap R^{-1}|$. Here $R\cap R^{-1}$ has $5$ diagonal pairs plus $(4,5),(5,4)$, so $7$: $n=16-7=9$.
For $xRy\iff ax\le by$ on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, row $x$ has $N-\lceil ax/b\rceil+1$ pairs (here $5-\lceil4x/5\rceil+1$: $5,4,3,2,2$). The relation is reflexive iff $a\le b$.
Pairs $(x,y)$ with both $4x\le5y$ and $4y\le5x$ form the symmetric part: here the diagonal and $(4,5),(5,4)$ ($7$ pairs); all other pairs of $R$ need their reverse added.

questions.question: Let $A=\{2,3,6,8,9,11\}$ and $B=\{1,4,5,10,15\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A\times B$ defined by $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d)$ if and only if $3ad-7bc$ is an even integer. Then the relation $R$ is: [JEE(Main) April 2024]
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.answer: (C) reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.key_idea: $3ad-7bc$ is even iff $ad+bc$ is even; this is symmetric in the two pairs, but transitivity fails.
solution: $(a,b)R(c,d)\iff 3ad-7bc$ is even.
Reflexive: $(a,b)R(a,b)$ gives $3ab-7ba=-4ab$, which is even. So $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: suppose $(a,b)R(c,d)$, so $3ad-7bc=(7ad-3bc)+(-4ad-4bc)$ is even. The term $-4ad-4bc$ is even, hence $7ad-3bc$ is even.
Then $(c,d)R(a,b)$ means $3bc-7ad=-(7ad-3bc)$ is even. True, so $R$ is symmetric.
Transitive? Take $(2,5)R(6,8)$: $3\cdot2\cdot8-7\cdot5\cdot6=48-210=-162$, even.
But $(2,5)R(9,4)$ needs $3\cdot2\cdot4-7\cdot5\cdot9=24-315=-291$, which is odd. So $(2,5)\not R(9,4)$ and $R$ is not transitive.
So $R$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: $(a,b)$ with both entries even is related to every element, so a transitive $R$ would force everything to be related; find an unrelated pair.
solution: Reduce mod $2$: $3ad-7bc\equiv ad+bc\pmod2$. So $(a,b)R(c,d)$ iff $ad+bc$ is even.
The element $(2,4)\in A\times B$ has both entries even. For any $(c,d)$: $ad+bc=2d+4c$ is even, so $(2,4)$ is related to every element, in both directions.
If $R$ were transitive, $(3,4)R(2,4)$ and $(2,4)R(2,1)$ would give $(3,4)R(2,1)$.
But for $(3,4)$ and $(2,1)$: $ad+bc=3\cdot1+4\cdot2=11$, odd. So $(3,4)\not R(2,1)$ and $R$ is not transitive.
Reflexivity ($-4ab$ even) and symmetry (the expression $ad+bc$ is unchanged on swapping the pairs) hold, so $R$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: (C).

useful_results: $3ad-7bc\equiv ad+bc\pmod2$ because odd coefficients can be replaced by $1$ modulo $2$.

If some element is related to every element, and the relation is not total, then the relation cannot be an equivalence relation (it would make all elements equivalent). Test: elements with both coordinates even here.

Equivalence relation check: reflexive $(a\,R\,a)$, symmetric $(a\,R\,b\Rightarrow b\,R\,a)$, transitive; one failing instance (with all three elements explicitly named and verified) is enough to reject.
A relation defined by a symmetric expression in the two arguments (here $ad+bc$) is automatically symmetric.

questions.question: In a survey of $220$ students of a higher secondary school, it was found that at least $125$ and at most $130$ students studied Mathematics; at least $85$ and at most $95$ studied Physics; at least $75$ and at most $90$ studied Chemistry; $30$ studied both Physics and Chemistry; $50$ studied both Chemistry and Mathematics; $40$ studied both Mathematics and Physics and $10$ studied none of these subjects. Let $m$ and $n$ respectively be the least and the most number of students who studied all the three subjects. Then $m+n$ is equal to ______. [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: Put $x$ students in all three; the Venn regions fix the total as a function of $x$, and the extreme set sizes plus $x\le30$ give the extreme $x$.
solution: Let $x$ students study all three subjects. The regions of the Venn diagram: only $M\cap P$ is $40-x$, only $P\cap C$ is $30-x$, only $C\cap M$ is $50-x$.
Case $M=130,\ P=95,\ C=90$ (the largest sets): only $M=40+x$, only $P=25+x$, only $C=10+x$.
Adding all regions and the $10$ outside: $(40+x)+(40-x)+(25+x)+(50-x)+x+(30-x)+(10+x)+10=205+x=220$, so $x=15$. This is the least value, $m=15$.
Case $M=125,\ P=85,\ C=75$ (the smallest sets): only $M=35+x$, only $P=15+x$, only $C=x-5$ and the total is $175+x=220$, so $x=45$.

But $x=45$ is impossible: $30$ students study both Physics and Chemistry, so $x\le30$ (also $30-x\ge0$). With $x=30$ the sets can be made to fit (e.g. $M=125,P=95,C=80$, regions all non-negative). So the greatest value is $n=30$.
Therefore $m+n=15+30=45$.
questions.correction_note: Printed working has (i) a typo '14-x' for the region $M\cap P$ only (should be $40-x$, as the totals $165+x=210$ show), and (ii) the labels reversed: it calls $x=30$ the minimum $m$ and $x=15$ the maximum $n$. Actually the largest sets give $x=15$, the least value; the smallest sets give $x=45$, which is capped at $30$ by the $P\cap C=30$ condition, so $n=30$. Also the cap at $30$ is not justified in the PDF. $m+n=45$ is unchanged. Brute force over all set sizes confirms $\min x=15$, $\max x=30$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate the regions: inclusion-exclusion gives $M+P+C=330-x$, and the given size ranges bound $x$.
solution: Students studying at least one subject: $220-10=210$.
Inclusion-exclusion: $210=M+P+C-(40+30+50)+x$, so $M+P+C=330-x$.
Also all three subjects lie inside Physics $\cap$ Chemistry, so $x\le30$. Hence $15\le x\le30$.
Both ends occur: $x=15$ with $(M,P,C)=(130,95,90)$ and $x=30$ with $M+P+C=300$, e.g. $(125,95,80)$; all Venn regions are then non-negative. So $m=15$, $n=30$ and $m+n=45$.

useful_results: Three-set inclusion-exclusion: $|M\cup P\cup C|=|M|+|P|+|C|-|M\cap P|-|P\cap C|-|C\cap M|+|M\cap P\cap C|$. Check: $M=\{1,2,3\},P=\{2,3,4\},C=\{3,4,5\}$: $9-2-2-1+1=5$.
Always combine the inclusion-exclusion bound with the trivial bound $|M\cap P\cap C|\le\min$ of the pairwise intersections; the formula alone can give an infeasible value ($45$ here).
Region 'only $M\cap P$' $=|M\cap P|-x$ must be non-negative; and each 'only $M$' region $=|M|-|M\cap P|-|M\cap C|+x\ge0$. Check feasibility at each extreme.
If a stated 'both' count includes the triple intersection (as here), the exclusive regions are 'both' minus $x$.

questions.question: Let $A=\{2,3,6,7\}$ and $B=\{4,5,6,8\}$. Let $R$ be a relation on $A\times B$ defined by $(a_1,b_1)\,R\,(a_2,b_2)$ if and only if $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2$. Then the number of elements in $R$ is ______. [JEE(Main) April 2024]
questions.key_idea: The condition rearranges to $a_1-b_1=b_2-a_2$, so the pair counts depend only on the differences $a-b$.
solution: $A\times B$ has $16$ elements; $R$ is a set of ordered pairs of these elements with $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2$.
Counting the pairs listed: $2+1+2+2+1+3+2+1+2+2+3+2+2=25$.
So the number of elements in $R$ is $25$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite as $(a_1-b_1)+(a_2-b_2)=0$ and count by the value of $d=a-b$ over the $16$ elements.
solution: $a_1+a_2=b_1+b_2\iff(a_1-b_1)+(a_2-b_2)=0$. Let $d=a-b$ for each element of $A\times B$.
Let $N(d)$ be the number of elements with value $d$: $N(-6)=N(-5)=N(-4)=N(0)=N(3)=1$, $N(-3)=N(-1)=N(1)=N(2)=2$, $N(-2)=3$ (total $16$).
An ordered pair is in $R$ iff its two elements have values $d$ and $-d$. So $|R|=\sum_dN(d)N(-d)$.
$d=0$: $1\cdot1=1$. $d=\pm1$: $N(1)N(-1)=4$ for each of the two orders, so $8$. $d=\pm2$: $N(2)N(-2)=6$, two orders, $12$. $d=\pm3$: $N(3)N(-3)=2$, two orders, $4$. Others give $0$.

useful_results: A relation of the form $f(x_1)+f(x_2)=g$-type on pairs can be turned into a sum over values: if $d_1+d_2=0$, then $|R|=\sum_dN(d)N(-d)$ (counting ordered pairs).
Reflexive pairs $(p,p)\in R$ need $2a=2b$, i.e. $a=b$; here only $(6,6)$ qualifies. The relation is symmetric because $a_1+a_2$ and $b_1+b_2$ are symmetric.
Before listing by hand, count by structure: here the multiset of $a-b$ is $\{-6,-5,-4,-3^2,-2^3,-1^2,0,1^2,2^2,3\}$ (check: total $16$).
